clue.text: Entertaining piece with a great view from seats in circle?

definitions.text: Entertaining piece with a great view from seats in circle?

parts.words: Entertaining piece with a great view from seats in circle
parts.note: surface reading: a show watched from the dress circle of a theatre; setter's reading: passenger cars riding round on a giant revolving wheel at a fairground

explanation.surface: A theatre show seen from the best seats in the dress circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circle' suggests the theatre balcony, but the seats really travel round a circle, and the entertainment is a fairground ride.
explanation.definitionFit: This big fairground attraction carries riders in cabins around a vertical rim, giving them panoramic views from the top.

clue.text: Old palmist regularly failing tests

parts.note: ex- means former or old

indicators.note: every other letter fails to appear, so only an evenly spaced set of letters survives

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of palmist

explanation.surface: An elderly fortune-teller keeps flunking her examinations.
explanation.definitionFit: Exams are formal assessments of knowledge, the plural noun matching the plural word tests.

clue.text: Shame about Flash, Queen single's cover

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a mo is a moment, a flash
R for Regina, queen

indicators.note: a cover sits on the outside, so only the outermost letters of the word before it are wanted

parts.note: first and last letters of single

explanation.surface: Embarrassment over a record sleeve for a single by the band Queen, whose song Flash was a hit.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen recorded the Flash theme, so the surface reads as music; R is the standard abbreviation for Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: Remorse is deep regret or guilt for wrongdoing, a close synonym of shame as a feeling.

clue.text: Problem with US university crest

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem
the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

explanation.surface: An American college is having trouble with its coat of arms.
explanation.definitionFit: The crest of a hill or mountain is its highest point, its peak or top.

clue.text: Ultimately, Sharon Horgan terribly bored by English sycophant

indicators.note: something bored by a drill has another thing driven into its middle
done terribly, the letters are badly jumbled into a different order
ultimately means at the very end, so the final letter of the next word is used

parts.note: last letter of Sharon
taken as written; with the N it is shuffled
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: The comedian Sharon Horgan is dreadfully bored by a flattering Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: Sharon Horgan is a real Irish comedy writer, so the surface reads as gossip about her; the hyphenated answer splits the letters at an unexpected point.
explanation.definitionFit: A hanger-on attaches to someone important to win favour, much as a fawning flatterer does.

clue.text: One elevated to a higher position in disbelief?

definitions.text: One elevated to a higher position
definitions.meaning: surface reading: someone promoted to a senior post
setter's reading: the part of the face that is raised when you cannot believe what you hear

explanation.surface: Someone amazed to find themselves promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elevated' sounds like promotion at work, but it describes a facial feature lifted in surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: People raise this arch of hair above the eye when sceptical or astonished, a physical sign of doubt.

clue.text: Conservationists hope to support inhabitant

indicators.note: in a down clue a supporting word sits underneath, so the first word goes on top of the second

parts.note: a national is a citizen or inhabitant of a country
to trust is to hope or expect

explanation.surface: Environmental campaigners hope to back a local resident.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust is a British charity that preserves historic houses, gardens and countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: This charity protects heritage buildings and landscape, so its members are preservationists of land and property.

clue.text: Match day paper?

parts.note: surface reading: a programme or newspaper for a football fixture; setter's reading: a match is a marriage, and the paper is thrown over the couple on their wedding day

explanation.surface: A sports fan picks up a programme on the day of the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' means a wedding pairing, not a sporting fixture.
explanation.definitionFit: Small pieces of coloured paper are thrown over newlyweds at weddings, so they are paper for a marriage day.

clue.text: Catch article on Rooney maybe in rag

indicators.note: in a down clue one part placed on another sits above it, so the first comes before the second

parts.note: to catch is to take
the definite article
Mickey Rooney was a Hollywood actor; 'maybe' marks him as one example

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about the footballer Wayne Rooney appears in a tabloid rag.
explanation.walkthrough: Rooney suggests the footballer Wayne, but the first name needed is that of the actor Mickey Rooney.
explanation.definitionFit: To rag someone is to tease them, and the British idiom take the mickey means to mock or make fun.

clue.text: Siren in hallway off and on — room emptied

indicators.note: switching off and on means letters are dropped and kept in turn

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of hallway

indicators.note: an emptied word has lost its contents, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: room without its inner letters

explanation.surface: A siren in a corridor keeps cutting out and coming back while a room is evacuated.
explanation.definitionFit: A siren is a loud warning device, and alarm names any such signal of danger.

clue.text: Met son in fantastic American state

indicators.note: something fantastic is fanciful and unreal, so these letters take on a new form

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
A is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Meeting a son in a wonderful part of the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Minnesota is one of the fifty constituent divisions of the United States, in the upper Midwest.

clue.text: Wearing navy perhaps, and working as a 28 Across?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: serving in the armed forces, the navy being one example
second meaning: employed as a domestic servant in a household

explanation.walkthrough: 28 Across is PARLOURMAID; 'navy' looks like a colour of clothing, but it is the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes both military duty in the forces and employment as a household domestic in a grand house.

clue.text: Rob Lowe's lead character entering all over the place

indicators.note: one thing entering another goes inside it

parts.note: rife means widespread, found everywhere

indicators.note: the leading character of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Lowe

explanation.surface: The actor Rob Lowe's starring role turns up everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Rob Lowe reads as the actor's name, but Rob is a verb and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To rifle is to ransack and steal from, so it means to rob a place.

clue.text: Figure in brown at the back — yellowish-brown

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so its final letter is wanted

parts.note: last letter of brown
umber is a yellowish-brown earth pigment

explanation.surface: A shape painted in brown with yellowish-brown at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure is a numeral or digit, which is a numeric symbol, so the two nouns are interchangeable.

clue.text: Swear into microphone? The essence of Cockney Rebel!

indicators.note: one thing put into another is placed inside it

parts.note: mic is short for microphone
to aver is to declare or swear

indicators.note: the essence is the heart, so the central letter of the word is used

parts.note: the middle letter of the seven-letter Cockney

explanation.surface: A shout into the mic captures the spirit of the band Cockney Rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney Rebel was a 1970s British band, so the last words look like one name; the essence of a seven-letter word is its fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A maverick is an independent-minded nonconformist who goes against the group, much like a rebel.

clue.text: Foreign Office guard checking British timepiece

parts.note: abbreviation for the British government's Foreign Office
B is the abbreviation for British
a watch is a guard or lookout

explanation.surface: A Foreign Office security guard keeps an eye on British citizens.
explanation.walkthrough: The Foreign Office is the UK government department for overseas affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A fob watch is a pocket watch on a chain, an old-fashioned kind of clock carried on the person.

clue.text: Team struggling to invade acclaim enemy lines?

indicators.note: invaders get inside a territory, so these letters go within the other word

parts.note: to hail is to acclaim

indicators.note: a struggling side is in disarray, so its letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A floundering army unit marches into hostile territory beyond the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enemy lines' looks military, but the lines are written ones from people who dislike you.
explanation.definitionFit: Hate mail is abusive letters, lines written by foes, with the question mark flagging the playful reading.

clue.text: Nothing behind small sofa

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring
your seat is your behind, your bottom

explanation.surface: There is nothing at the back of a little couch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' looks like a position word, but it is a noun meaning the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A loveseat is a two-person couch, a compact upholstered settee built for a pair.

clue.text: A little prissy, ring assistant for lilac

indicators.note: only a little of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: letters running across the end of prissy, all of ring and the start of assistant

explanation.surface: A fussy boxing second picks out a pale purple colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Syringa is the botanical genus name of the lilac shrub, the flowering plant itself.

clue.text: Recalled Greek character unwell after a plant such as garlic

indicators.note: after places the preceding group behind the single word that follows

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: recalled things are called back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet
ill means unwell

explanation.surface: A sick Greek is recalled from duty after eating a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Allium is the genus of onions, leeks and chives, of which garlic is the best-known member.

clue.text: Terribly glum about dispute over angler's bait

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned over means flipped so it reads upwards
about means surrounding, so one group goes round the other
done terribly, the letters end up muddled into another order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a row is an argument

explanation.surface: A fisherman is miserable over a quarrel about his bait.
explanation.definitionFit: Lugworms are marine worms dug from sand and mudflats for sea anglers to put on hooks.

clue.text: So long in spot close to Banbury and Oxford University

parts.note: to spot is to see

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so the final letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of Banbury
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A long stretch spent in a place near Banbury and Oxford's colleges.
explanation.walkthrough: Banbury is an English town north of Oxford, so the surface reads as geography.
explanation.definitionFit: So long is an informal farewell, and see you is another casual parting phrase used when leaving.

clue.text: Sinatra rereleases somewhat less common

indicators.note: somewhat means only partly, so just part of the words is used

parts.note: letters spanning the end of Sinatra and the start of rereleases

explanation.surface: Frank Sinatra's records reissued are a little scarcer.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end and the indicator, somewhat, sits between the fodder and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rarer is the comparative of rare, meaning more unusual, which is exactly what less common expresses.

clue.text: Full of beans and windy, get niece to bring in last of Alka-Seltzer

indicators.note: letters brought in are taken inside the other group
windy weather blows things about, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter of Alka-Seltzer

explanation.surface: Someone bloated from eating beans asks a niece to fetch an antacid.
explanation.walkthrough: Alka-Seltzer is a fizzy indigestion remedy, which suits the beans and wind in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of beans is an idiom for lively and bouncy, which matches being vigorous and active.

clue.text: It's over, after initially thanking United trainer and all the players

indicators.note: after puts the reversed word behind the group that follows
initially points to the first letter of each of the following words

parts.note: first letters of thanking, United and trainer

indicators.note: turned over in a down clue, the word reads upwards

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: The match is finished, and a football coach thanks the whole squad.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of It's stands for is, joining the reversal indicator. Tutti is a musical direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutti is the Italian musical term marking a passage played by the whole orchestra together.

clue.text: Inferior candy store with no Tango, sadly

indicators.note: things that go sadly go wrong, so the letters are put in a different arrangement
with no means lacking, so a letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
Tango is T in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A second-rate sweet shop sadly has run out of the orange fizzy drink Tango.
explanation.walkthrough: Tango is a British fizzy soft drink, but here it is the radio-alphabet word for T.
explanation.definitionFit: Secondary means lesser in rank or quality, so it works as a synonym of inferior.

clue.text: Strange and unpopular ref getting France eliminated?

parts.note: out of fashion, unpopular

indicators.note: something eliminated is knocked out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
F is the international code for France

explanation.surface: An odd and disliked referee gets France knocked out of a tournament.
explanation.definitionFit: Outré is a French loan word for bizarre or unconventional, beyond the bounds of what is normal.

clue.text: According to Spooner, composer Gustav gave money to female servant

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of two words trade places

parts.note: Gustav Mahler is the composer; said with the P from the start of the other word in place of his M
gave money is paid; said with the M from the composer in place of its P

explanation.surface: The composer Mahler paid wages to a maid.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of Mahler paid to get parler maid, which says PARLOURMAID.
explanation.definitionFit: A parlourmaid was a woman employed in a household to wait at table and serve in the reception rooms.
